newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel expects compromise on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel expects compromise on NATO expansion.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Saturday NATO would have to compromise at its Madrid summit between the U.S. view that only three new members should be admitted and a European lobby for five.
Kinkel told SFB radio the U.S. position was by no means the final word on the issue.

"We have to find a compromise between the massive support for five new members and the massive position of the Americans," Kinkel said. "Naturally, America's word carries weight. But a preliminary decision has not yet been made."

Kinkel said Germany, which has stayed officially noncommital on the size of the eastern enlargement, was heading to the July 8-9 Madrid summit with an open mind and would not let itself be pushed around for the "wrong reasons" by the "wrong side". He did not say which side he thought was "wrong".
Kinkel has said that three, four or five former Warsaw Pact nations could be added in the first wave of enlargement while German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe has expressed a preference for three.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at the summit.
While the United States wants to limit the first enlargement to those three, many European NATO members want Slovenia and Romania included.

"As an important country, we have considered very carefully our position," Kinkel said. "It is no secret that Volker Ruehe is in favour of three new members because of military reasons. I can understand that.
"But the decision on which countries join NATO is primarily a political decision," he added.
President Bill Clinton has said only the three are currently ready for membership, but pledged to leave open the door to other central and eastern European states to join at a later date.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said in Madrid on Saturday he could not yet set a firm timetable for future expansion of the alliance.
"There is no commitment, not today, maybe tomorrow. There will be another summit in 1999 to evaluate it," he told reporters.
Solana said NATO members had not yet reached a consensus on whether to include three, four or five former Soviet allies, but added he was confident a compromise would be found.
NATO says only countries with a mixed economy and a functioning democracy, including democratic control of the armed forces, and with no disputes with neighbouring states can even be considered.

Supporters of enlargement say even a limited expansion will erase forever the artificial division of Europe created by the Cold War and inaugurate a new era of European security with NATO at its centre.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl last week said he supported Romania's bid to join NATO soon, but said he believed the decision on how many countries join the alliance should be made by all 16 NATO members in Madrid.

In a separate interview with SDR radio to be broadcast on Sunday, the foreign policy spokesman of Kohl's Christian Democrats, Rudolf Seiters, said he expected that the United States' position would prevail in Madrid.
